test.title: Section 3 · the long road of the zip

texts.title: The slow triumph of the zip

paragraphs.text: Most useful objects are invented once and adopted quickly. The zip took sixty years. The first version was shown at a world fair in 1893 as a fastener for boots, and it worked so badly that the inventor spent the rest of his life redesigning it: the hooks sprang open at the wrong moment, and a fastener that opens by itself on a boot is worse than a row of buttons. Nothing about the early history suggests an object that would one day be sewn into billions of garments a year.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The design that worked arrived in 1913 and owed almost nothing to the original. Instead of hooks it used identical metal teeth, each with a dimple on one side and a matching bump on the other, drawn together by a slider that bent them into place. The change was quiet and complete: nothing in the new fastener could spring open, because nothing in it was under tension when closed. The engineer who made it spent the following decade not on the fastener but on the machine that could produce its teeth quickly and identically enough to be sold cheaply.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Even then, clothing would not take it. The first large orders came from the American army, which used the fastener on flying suits and money belts during the First World War, and from the makers of rubber galoshes, who needed something that could be closed with one hand while holding an umbrella. It was a galosh manufacturer who gave the object its name, taken from the sound it made. The name was a trademark for a boot, not for the fastener, which is why a word that began as a brand became the ordinary English for the thing itself.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Clothing resisted for reasons that had little to do with engineering. Tailors distrusted a fastener they could not repair with a needle, and a garment with a broken zip was thrown away rather than mended, which looked like waste to a generation that mended everything. Buttons were also cheaper. Children’s clothes were the opening: parents liked anything a four-year-old could manage alone, and a generation of children who grew up with zips became adults who expected them. The change in menswear came in the 1930s and was helped by a fashion magazine that praised trouser zips for exactly that reason.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The industry that grew around the object is stranger than the object. Because a zip must open ten thousand times without failing, the tolerances are tighter than in much of the clothing trade, and the machines that make the teeth are expensive; the result is a market dominated by a small number of very large manufacturers. One Japanese company alone makes something close to half the zips in the world, and it makes its own brass, its own thread and many of its own machines, on the grounds that a fastener is only as reliable as its worst component.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The zip has had one serious rival, and it lost more ground than expected. Hook-and-loop tape, patented in the 1950s after its inventor looked at burrs under a microscope, is quicker to fasten and needs no alignment, which is why it took over children’s shoes and medical clothing. But it collects lint, it is noisy, it fails when wet and it cannot bear much load across the closure, so it never seriously threatened the trouser fly or the suitcase. The two objects divided the world between them within about fifteen years and have barely moved since.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Repair has come back, which changes the argument that kept tailors suspicious. A zip that fails usually fails at the slider rather than the teeth, and a slider can be replaced in a few minutes with a tool that costs very little; clothing brands that now offer repair have found that the majority of garments sent back to them need exactly this. The waste argument has therefore reversed: a garment fastened with a zip is easier to bring back into use than one fastened with a moulded plastic clip, which cannot be replaced at all when it snaps.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: What the story shows is how slowly an obviously better object can spread. Every part of the delay had a reason: the first design did not work, the second had no machine to make it, the third had no customers who trusted it, and the fourth had to wait for children to grow up. The sixty years look absurd only in hindsight, when the intermediate steps have been forgotten and the object seems to have been inevitable from the start.
paragraphs.label: H
